## Foundation

Small shared mechanics: Python API behavior, failure telemetry, cell
parsing, validation, chapter navigation, and dynamic cell classification
for notebook context.

This notebook is the shared basement of the project. It keeps the small
private helpers that every public tool relies on: Python API behavior,
safe error reporting, cell selection, cell parsing, semantic cell
classification, and chapter addressing.

Most functions here are intentionally private. The rest of the project
can stay user-facing because this notebook absorbs the messy details of
notebooks as data structures.

Read it as a tour of the shapes nbskill needs to recognize. A notebook
is not just text: it has cells, headings, generated Python files,
visible outputs, and tiny bits of metadata. The foundation layer gives
all later notebooks one vocabulary for those shapes, so the public tools
can talk about notebooks without making users think in raw JSON.

### Production contract

This notebook owns the shared invariants for every other tool.
Production behavior is: path helpers resolve notebooks from project-root
and notebook-dir execution, cell-block parsing creates valid notebook
cells, metadata stamping records semantic classes and export hashes, and
validation reports missing or stale metadata before edits proceed.

The helpers here deliberately stay small because every higher-level tool
depends on them. For example,
[`parse_cells`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#parse_cells)
turns friendly cell-block text into notebook cells, the semantic
classifiers let readers say “show me tests” or “show me exported code”
without parsing raw notebook JSON.

### Demo scratch files

Examples and tests in later notebooks need small notebooks they can
safely mutate. Scratch helpers create disposable artifacts in the system
temporary directory and remove them after use, so notebook test runners
never create repository data folders.
[`tool_notebook`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#tool_notebook)
builds the shared reader, executor, reviewer, and MCP example shape in
code.

instead of repeating `try`/`finally` in every test.

Here is the tiny notebook fixture in the wild. It gives examples a real
`.ipynb` to read, then vanishes after the context exits, which keeps the
repo tidy while still letting the rendered notebook show concrete
output.

``` python
from fastcore.nbio import read_nb

with write_demo_notebook("00_foundation_tour.ipynb") as path:
    nb = read_nb(path)
    print(path.name)
    print([cell.cell_type for cell in nb.cells])
    print(str(nb.cells[0].source).splitlines()[0])

print(path.exists())
```

## Generated source ownership

nbdev can place a module docstring before its autogenerated-file notice.
Source ownership therefore finds the notice in the exported text instead
of assuming that it is in the first three physical lines. This keeps
generated modules read-only for agents.

### Parsing user-facing selectors

Selectors are the boundary between human shorthand and list operations.
A caller might ask for `3`, `2:5`, `-1`, or `None`; these helpers
normalize that text before any read or write tool touches notebook
cells. Keeping the grammar here makes higher-level tools predictable and
keeps cell-index mistakes from spreading.

### Turning text into notebook cells

Write tools accept plain text because that is what agents and humans can
produce quickly. This section turns that text into real cells: split on
block separators, honor `%%markdown`/`%%code` markers, and split
exported code into symbol-sized chunks when needed. It is the small
parser that makes notebook edits feel like editing a document instead of
assembling JSON.

### Cell metadata and semantic classes

Once cells can be parsed, the tools need names for what they *are
doing*. A code cell with output is an example; a code cell with an
`assert` is a test; a markdown cell with prose is documentation. Those
labels power filters such as `type=tests` and help review tools talk
about notebooks in human terms.

### Domain entities

These tiny models give the project names for the shapes it already
manipulates: cells, chapters, notebooks, and symbols. The classes stay
thin; most behavior is patched onto them so each concept can grow near
the helper that understands it.

### Typed cell vocabularies

[`CellType`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#celltype)
names the three notebook cell kinds,
[`SemanticType`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#semantictype)
names the reader-facing role a cell plays, and
[`Directive`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#directive)
names the nbdev directives an editor can stamp onto a cell. Enums keep
the rest of the project from passing bare strings around, and let
context drop directive lines because the type already carries that
meaning.

### Notebook document helpers

[`NotebookDocument.cell`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#notebookdocument.cell)
returns one cell model by id. `chapter` resolves a heading-owned span,
`notebook_source_hash` gives the model’s stable source hash, and
`commit` sends the current model through
[`commit_notebook`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#commit_notebook).

``` python
document = NotebookDocument(new_nb([mk_cell("## Alpha", cell_type="markdown"), mk_cell("answer = 42")]), path="demo.ipynb")
(document.cell(document.nb.cells[1].id).source, document.chapter("Alpha").title, document.notebook_source_hash())
```

The notebook domain model gives callers small, navigable objects:
`Notebook.cell` finds a stable cell id, `Notebook.chapter` returns a
dynamic
[`Chapter`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#chapter),
`Notebook.notebook_source_hash` summarizes ordered source, and
`Notebook.commit` writes through the same atomic path as the editing
tools.

### Project-scoped nbdev export

[`run_nbdev_export_from_project`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#run_nbdev_export_from_project)
and
[`export_notebook`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#export_notebook)
deliberately run nbdev export in an isolated process under a
project-scoped lock. This looks heavier than calling `nbdev_export`
directly, but it protects the MCP server when several repositories on
the same computer are edited at the same time.

The two failures this avoids are subtle. First, nbdev export depends on
project context; changing the server process cwd with `os.chdir` is
global state, so concurrent exports from different projects can race.
Second, an MCP client timeout does not stop a Python worker thread, so a
timed-out edit can keep exporting in the background and consume memory.
A child process is a boundary the caller can terminate, while the lock
only serializes exports for the same project. Different projects get
different lock files and can still make progress independently.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/MorsCerta-crypto/nbskill/blob/main/nbskill/foundation.py#L1449"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### Stable ids and notebook commits

[`ensure_cell_ids`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#ensure_cell_ids)
fills in missing notebook cell ids.
[`notebook_hash`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#notebook_hash)
changes when a cell’s id or source changes.
[`commit_notebook`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#commit_notebook)
validates and records a proposed notebook change, or writes and exports
it when `dry_run` is false.

``` python
trial = new_nb([mk_cell("value = 1")])
ensure_cell_ids(trial)
commit_notebook("nbs/data/commit_notebook_example.ipynb", trial, dry_run=True, export=False)["planned_hash"] == notebook_hash(trial)
```

[`notebook_hash`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#notebook_hash)
and
[`commit_notebook`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#commit_notebook)
form the shared commit primitive. Callers build a trial notebook, pass
the original as `before`, and get read-back hashes after the write
succeeds. The commit boundary rejects malformed notebook structure and
duplicate cell ids before it writes. Changed code-cell outputs are
cleared before the notebook is committed.

### Naming cells by behavior

The reading and MCP layers present cells by meaning, not just by `code`
or `markdown`. This section detects imports, private helpers, exported
code, tests, examples, docs, section headers, and mixed cells so callers
can filter notebooks at a useful level. A test that produces a useful
output is intentionally both a test and an example; that pairing is not
an unclean mixed cell.

``` python
from fastcore.nbio import read_nb

with write_demo_notebook("commit_notebook_example.ipynb", cells=[mk_cell(chr(10).join(["value = 1", "print(value)"]))]) as commit_path:
    before_nb = read_nb(commit_path)
    trial_nb = read_nb(commit_path)
    print(notebook_hash(before_nb))
    trial_nb.cells[0].source = chr(10).join(["value = 2", "print(value)"])
    trial_nb.cells[0].outputs = [dict(output_type="stream", name="stdout", text="stale" + chr(10))]
    result = commit_notebook(commit_path, trial_nb, before=before_nb, affected_cell_ids=[trial_nb.cells[0].id], export=False)
    print(result["changed"], result["affected_cell_ids"])
    print(read_nb(commit_path).cells[0].outputs)
```

[`parse_cells`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#parse_cells)
is the little translator between a friendly edit format and real
notebook cells. The dashed line means “start a new cell”, while
`%%markdown` and `%%code` make the intended cell type explicit.

``` python
_demo_text = "\n".join(["%%markdown", "## Demo", "---", "%%code", "value = 42"])
_demo_cells = parse_cells(_demo_text)
for idx, cell in enumerate(_demo_cells):
    print(cell_prefix(idx, cell))
    print("  type:", cell.cell_type)
    print("  first line:", first_line(cell_source(cell)))
```

      type: markdown
      first line: ## Demo
    Cell id=38f08303: code
      type: code

### Visible cell output

[`output_value_text`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#output_value_text),
[`output_text`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#output_text),
and
[`cell_output_text`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#cell_output_text)
turn Jupyter output payloads into plain text.
[`Cell.output_text`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#cell.output_text),
[`Cell.semantic_type`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#cell.semantic_type),
and
[`Cell.context_record`](https://MorsCerta-crypto.github.io/nbskill/foundation.html#cell.context_record)
apply the same rules to a cell model used by readers.

``` python
output_cell = mk_cell("print('ok')")
output_cell.outputs = [dict(output_type="stream", name="stdout", text="ok\n")]
output_model = Cell(output_cell, idx=4)
(output_value_text(["o", "k"]), output_text(output_cell.outputs[0]), cell_output_text(output_cell), output_model.output_text(), output_model.semantic_type(), output_model.context_record()["cell_idx"])
```

### Chapters as editing scopes

Chapters are the notebook-native version of a module section. A heading
cell opens a span, and everything until the next heading belongs to that
span. Write, execute, and read tools use these spans so users can say
“the query language chapter” instead of counting cell indexes by hand.

``` python
with write_demo_notebook("domain_model_example.ipynb", cells=[mk_cell("## Alpha", cell_type="markdown"), mk_cell("answer = 42")]) as model_path:
    model_doc = Notebook.from_path(model_path)
    model_cell = model_doc.cell(model_doc.nb.cells[1].id)
    model_chapter = model_doc.chapter("Alpha")
    print(model_cell.source)
    print(model_chapter.to_record())
    print(model_doc.notebook_source_hash())
    print(model_doc.commit(before=model_doc.nb, export=False)["changed"])
```

On a real notebook, chapter spans become a tiny table of contents with
cell ranges. Here `index.ipynb` is being parsed by the foundation
helpers that the reading tools themselves rely on.

``` python
_index_cells = read_nb("index.ipynb").cells
for span in chapter_spans(_index_cells)[:5]: print(f"{span['title']}: cells {span['start']}..{span['end'] - 1}")

print("reading indexes:", sorted(chapter_index_set(_index_cells, "Reading"))[:5])
```

    The problem this project solves: cells 2..2
    How the notebooks fit together: cells 3..3
    Production readiness: cells 4..5
    A tiny notebook to work on: cells 6..7
    Reading: choose the smallest useful context: cells 8..9
    reading indexes: [8, 9]

``` python
one = parse_one_cell("%%code\nvalue = 99")
assert one.cell_type == "code"
assert one.source == "value = 99"
encoded = "def f():" + chr(92) + "n    return 1"
assert load_cells_text("%%code\\nvalue = 1") == "%%code\\nvalue = 1"
assert load_cells_text(encoded) == encoded
```

Here are the labels on toy cells. This is deliberately small, but it is
the same classification that lets the reading and review tools
distinguish examples from tests without asking a model to guess.

``` python
public_cell = mk_cell("#| export\ndef public():\n    return 1")
private_cell = mk_cell("#| export\ndef _private():\n    return 1")
example_cell = mk_cell("value = 1")
example_cell.outputs = [dict(output_type="stream", name="stdout", text="1\n")]
for label, cell in {"public": public_cell, "private": private_cell, "example": example_cell}.items():
    print(f"{label:8} -> {', '.join(cell_class_names(cell))}")
```

The tests below define the complete semantic contract: public and
private exported symbols, multicells, output-bearing tests, examples,
documentation, titles, metadata refresh, and the only allowed mixed role
(`test_code` plus `example_code`).

A semantic cell gets explicit source-and-output roles. Imports
distinguish `exported_import_cell` from `internal_import_cell`; a
visible test is the only allowed `test_code` + `example_code`
combination. `multicell` is reserved for a cell with multiple
differently named top-level functions, public or private. Every other
mixed role is a writing warning.

Metadata stamping is separate from classification: it records the
generated Python artifact and caches the semantic labels that downstream
tools can reuse.

Python API helpers return values directly and raise `ValueError` for
invalid inputs; notebook execution stays independent of process
arguments.
